params.text:
Confidentiality is not the same as secrecy

Confidentiality means personal information is shared only with those who have a genuine need to know it for the person’s care. It does not mean information is never shared at all. Sometimes sharing is exactly the right thing to do — for example, passing a change in someone’s condition to a nurse or GP.

The skill is knowing what to share, with whom, and why. Share too little and a person may not get safe care; share too widely and you break both their trust and the law.

The Caldicott principles

The Caldicott principles are a well-known guide for handling confidential health and care information. They help you judge when sharing is appropriate. In short, they remind you to:

  • Justify the purpose: be clear about why information is being shared.
  • Use only what is needed: share the minimum amount necessary.
  • Share on a need-to-know basis: only with those involved in the person’s care.
  • Respect duties both ways: the duty to share can matter as much as the duty to protect.
  • Follow the law: everyone handling information should understand their responsibilities.

A further principle reminds services to be open with people about how their information is used.

Storing, keeping and disposing of records

Care records contain sensitive personal information, so they must be handled securely for as long as you hold them — and disposed of safely when they are no longer needed.

  • Secure storage: keep paper records locked away, and never leave electronic records open on an unattended screen.
  • Retention: keep records only as long as they are needed. Adult social care records are generally kept for a minimum of eight years, following your organisation’s retention policy.
  • Disposal: dispose of records securely — shred paper and delete electronic files properly — never in ordinary bins or recycling.

params.textField: *Confidentiality* means sharing personal information only with those who genuinely need it. Sharing on a *need-to-know* basis limits who can see a person’s details. The Caldicott principles say you should share the *minimum* amount of information necessary. Sometimes the duty to *share* is as important as the duty to protect. Being *open* with people about how their information is used helps build trust.

params.question: Which of these follow the rules on confidentiality, storage and retention? (Select all that apply.)

answers.text: Sharing information only with those who need it to support the person.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The "need to know" principle is central to confidentiality under UK GDPR.

answers.text: Logging in as yourself on the electronic system and never sharing your password.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Your login identifies who made each entry, so it must never be shared.

answers.text: Leaving a paper care file open on the kitchen table between visits.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This breaches confidentiality and secure-storage duties. Records must be kept locked away.

answers.text: Keeping records securely for the retention period, then disposing of them by shredding.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Records are kept for the required period, then destroyed securely rather than binned.
